articles.title: Trump hopes to flatter Putin into negotiating on Ukraine, experts say
articles.author: Peter Nicholas

paras.en: WASHINGTON — In recent weeks, President Donald Trump has taken measures that strengthen Russia’s position and may rehabilitate Russian President Vladimir Putin’s soiled reputation in the international community.

Trump returned to office vowing to swiftly end the Russia-Ukraine war, proclaiming last year that he was on “nobody’s side” except “humanity’s side.” But the neutral posture he said he has adopted is peeling away.

A specific strategic goal underlies Trump’s overtures to Putin, foreign policy experts said. The idea is to entice him to come to the negotiating table and end a war that is now in its fifth year. Whether it will work is another question.

Trump’s lead negotiator in the Russia-Ukraine war, Steve Witkoff, called Putin “a humanitarian” in St. Petersburg on Wednesday upon the release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had detained since 2022. Even Republican lawmakers balked at the remark.
Witkoff thanks Putin for release of retired American teacher
“I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He’s certainly not a humanitarian,” Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is in a tough fight for re-election, said Wednesday.
“He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine,” she added at a campaign stop at a factory in Norway, Maine.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who isn’t running for re-election following public disagreements with Trump, was blunter. “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” he posted on social media.

Freedom House, a nonprofit that works to expand freedom and democracy, describes Russia as an authoritarian country where power is “concentrated in the hands of President Vladimir Putin.” The Kremlin “manipulates elections and suppresses genuine dissent,” the group says.

Trump tends to see diplomacy through the prism of personal relations, and he has made no secret of his regard for Putin. When he hosted Putin for a summit meeting in Alaska last year in a futile attempt to end the war, the U.S. rolled out a red carpet. A picture of Trump and Putin standing side by side hangs in the White House’s Palm Room.

By contrast, Trump has stepped up his on-again, off-again criticism of Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As he left the White House on Monday for a campaign trip, he said Zelenskyy “is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”
Blandishments are a tool Trump is using to get Putin to strike a deal, said Robert O’Brien, who was White House national security adviser in Trump’s first term. Not much else has worked.

“We thought we could get the war settled two years ago, but Putin has been intractable in not coming to the table. President Trump is using cordiality to get Putin to negotiate,” O’Brien said in an interview.
“There’d be no hope of getting Putin to engage in talks, with the U.S. as the mediator, if he viewed Trump as 100% aligned with Ukraine in this situation,” he added.

Michael Kimmage, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution think tank, said the Trump administration’s “theory of the case is that by distancing themselves from Ukraine and by flattering the Russians, they can accomplish something at the bargaining table.”
He doesn’t expect the gambit to succeed, though.

“In the absence of a clear agenda coming from the White House and in the absence of very serious forms of leverage over Russia — which the Trump administration has shied away from — progress at the negotiating table is very difficult to imagine,” he said.

Asked about Trump’s warmer attitude toward Putin in recent weeks, the White House pointed to his comments at a roundtable on cybercrime when he was asked about Witkoff labeling the Russian leader “a humanitarian.”
Trump responded: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose — for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out.”

He went on to add that the U.S. is negotiating with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and was complimentary towards Russia for having “not gotten involved with Iran.” Trump said that some “stupid people” were critical of his position and “the last thing I want to do is upset an apple cart where we’re getting close to settling a war.”

Ending the war between Russia and Ukraine was one of Trump’s signature promises in the 2024 campaign. He had confidently predicted he’d get it done on his first day back in office, but he has since conceded that the problem is more stubborn than he’d envisioned.
As Trump works to broker a peace deal, one of his recent gestures to Putin is to treat him as a statesman, rather than a global outcast.

Trump thanked Putin on Oct. 9 after they reached a deal in which Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel into global markets. Trump said the move would ease energy costs, but relief at the pump hasn’t happened yet. Since then, the average price of a gallon of diesel has risen 4 cents a gallon, from $6.26 to $6.30.

Trump invited Putin to attend the G20 international summit meeting at his Doral golf resort in Miami, and he said this week that he’s open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss nuclear weapons.

A summit meeting alongside the leaders of the world’s two largest economies would be a boon to Putin, whom the West has ostracized since Russia invaded Crimea in 2014. World leaders expelled Putin from an elite international organization called the G8 after that attack.
“There’s no question that Trump has been trying to reintegrate Putin into polite society,” said Brett Bruen, who was director of global engagement in the Obama White House.
At the G20 summit at Trump’s golf club in December, Putin would be “the shiny object that Trump would dangle in front of the world press corps as purported progress toward peace,” Bruen said.

A question Europeans are asking is what sort of peace deal does Trump visualize. Would it be fair to Ukraine or carve up the country at Putin’s behest, they ask? If Ukraine ceded territory to Putin as the price of ending the war, that would only embolden him to threaten more states, a European official said.

Marko Mihkelson, chairman of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee in Estonia, which borders Russia, said in an interview: “If you reward aggressors” and signal that they can “achieve their goals through aggression, then that doesn’t stop them from continuing.”

Faced with a war in Iran that he started and a war in Europe that he can’t stop, Trump is advised by a thinning inner circle. A senior aide, press secretary Karoline Leavitt, left the White House over the summer. Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., one of Trump’s confidants and a Russia hawk, died unexpectedly in July.
Two months later, Trump signed a bill named after Graham that sanctioned Russian officials and parts of the country’s economy.
Trump waived those sanctions last week — which Graham might have warned against in their many phone calls and golf games.
“Lindsey Graham is rolling over in his grave,” Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., told reporters Wednesday.

articles.title: Accused High Country killer applies for bail claiming he has been attacked in jail
articles.author: Kristian Silva

paras.en: Greg Lynn, who is accused of murdering retiree Carol Clay in Victoria's High Country, says he has been threatened and "shitbombed" by fellow prisoners.
The 60-year-old entered the witness box today during his application for bail.
In order to be freed on bail, Mr Lynn's lawyers must prove there are exceptional circumstances that justify his release.
Accused High Country killer Greg Lynn wants to be freed on bail, claiming he has been subjected to attacks in custody and because he believes fellow inmates are police informers.
Mr Lynn, 60, stepped into the Victorian Supreme Court witness box today during his bail application.
In the hearing, he told Chief Justice Richard Niall he had been "shitbombed" in his cell by a fellow prisoner in 2024, while he was being held at the Melbourne Assessment Prison.
"He had an empty milk bottle which he'd filled with faeces and other disgusting material, bodily fluids, and he threw that," he said.
"Some of it went all over me. I had to go straight to my cell and rinse under the shower for a long, long time.
Accused tells court of attack by fellow prisoner
Mr Lynn also told the court of incidents in July this year at the Metropolitan Remand Centre, where he is currently being held.
He said a prisoner made threats towards him when he refused to be placed in a holding cell with the man.
"He was ready to explode. He was like Mount Vesuvius ready to erupt," Mr Lynn said.
"He mentioned that he'd killed people before and he'd kill again.
"Then he said I was a killer of old people."
Mr Lynn said he denied the accusation and returned to his cell.
During another confrontation with the same person, Mr Lynn said he called the man a police informer.
The man responded by poking him in the chest and spitting at him, Mr Lynn said.
"I am the victim here. I am the target of this informant," Mr Lynn told the court.
Mr Lynn — dressed in a lavender shirt, tie and dark suit — was supported in court by his wife Melanie and eldest son Geordie Lynn.

The former Jetstar pilot wants to live with Geordie ahead of a trial in mid-2027, over the alleged murder of retiree Carol Clay at a remote Victorian campsite in 2020. Ms Clay’s companion Russell Hill also died at the campsite.
On Thursday, Mr Lynn’s barrister Dermot Dann said his client had been cleared of Mr Hill’s death, and should be given the “full benefit of the acquittal” at the upcoming trial.
Mr Lynn has always maintained his innocence, arguing he was not criminally responsible for what happened to the pair.
Having been in custody since 2021, Mr Lynn testified he was "hated" by fellow inmates at the Metropolitan Remand Centre, many of whom he had never met.
After the July altercation with the prisoner in the Deakin B protection unit, prisoners hurled "every insult" at him for about an hour, Mr Lynn said.
"What a worthless dog I was, I was going to be stabbed, I was going to be bashed," he said.
Corrections staff willing to relocate accused, court hears
Mr Lynn said he felt unsafe in the unit and with other protection unit options put forward by Corrections Victoria.
Mr Lynn also believed other prisoners were willing to provide false statements about him to police, the court heard.
"They would clearly lie about their own mother for a sentence discount," he said.

A Corrections Victoria manager, Anthony Calandro, said footage of the July incident was viewed and staff did not see any evidence of Mr Lynn being attacked. The complaint was reported to Victoria Police and the footage wiped, he said.
Mr Calandro said Corrections Victoria was willing to work with Mr Lynn to relocate him to another prison, but could not do so if he continued to accuse other prisoners of being informers.
Mr Lynn said conditions in one of the units he was held in were "draconian", resulting in 23-hour lockdowns each day.
While addressing Mr Lynn's proposed bail, the former pilot said a concern had been raised about his wife holding an airport security pass because of her job as a flight attendant.
"The concern is that I will steal Melanie's security pass and do something at the airport, I don't know what," he said.
"I would not pass as a tall, thin, blonde female.
"What would I do with the pass, steal an aeroplane? It's ridiculous."
In order to be freed on bail, Mr Lynn's lawyers must show the court there are exceptional circumstances that justify his release and that he does not pose an unacceptable risk to the community.
Mr Lynn's barrister, Dermot Dann KC, said the prosecution would not be alleging his client posed an unacceptable risk.
Among the compelling reasons for bail, Mr Dann cited the lengthy period Mr Lynn had spent on remand, solitary confinement conditions, and the support of his family.
Prosecutors are expected to address the court later today.

articles.title: SA mother spared jail for 6yo daughter's death in car crash
articles.author: Jordanna Schriever

paras.en: A judge has promised not to imprison a mother, who pleaded guilty to causing her six-year-old daughter's death in a road crash at Virginia last year.
The girl's father told the court that their children "need their mother's love, care, guidance and support".
Ms Habonimana will be sentenced next month.
A mother who got lost on the way to church before failing to give way at an intersection – causing a crash which killed her own child – will not be sent to prison, a court has heard.
Zubeda Habonimana, 43, was driving a white van which struck a ute at the intersection of King and Penfield roads, at Virginia in Adelaide's northern suburbs, on October 5 last year.
Her six-year-old daughter Benita Ntihebuwayo suffered catastrophic injuries and died five days after the crash, while two of her other children and the driver of the ute were injured.
Father tells court children need their mother

In victim impact statements read in South Australia's District Court today, Benita's father Jason Birgirmana described the lasting impact of the loss of his daughter, but asked the court not to send his former partner to jail.
"Losing our baby was an extremely painful experience for all of us and the impact of this tragedy continues to affect our lives,"
Mr Birgirmana said their other children "continue to need their mother's love, care, guidance and support", particularly while coping with the loss of their sibling.

"I am capable of looking after my children, and I am a good father, but I also understand the important role and connection my children have with their mother, which can look different to what I can provide my children," he said.
The driver of the ute, Jason Pateman, told the court his life had "been in complete turmoil" since the crash, and that he continued to grapple with the life-changing impacts of a severe concussion.
He had been driving to Bunnings with his four-year-old daughter when they were struck.
"The sound of my daughter screaming in the car will haunt me every single day," he said.
He said while his daughter's injuries were not physical, the impact on her wellbeing had been "huge".
He said he could not forgive Habonimana, but did not wish her any harm.
"I spent weeks crying over the loss of your child. I know, it wasn't my fault, we were simply in the wrong place at the wrong time, but as a parent, it destroyed me emotionally,"
"I don’t want you in prison as I don't want your family to suffer further, but I do believe you should never be allowed to operate a motor vehicle again.
"The day your child passed away, you gave yourself a life sentence. No further punishment would be comparable."
His wife Tamika Pateman also detailed the lasting impacts on their daughter form being exposed to a "violent and chaotic scene".
"Things that used to be completely ordinary are now frightening to her," she said.
Habonimana previously pleaded guilty to one count of causing death and three counts of causing harm by dangerous driving.
The mother of seven's defence counsel Andrew Ey said the punishment his client had suffered was "immeasurable".
"She has agonised over this, but she can't explain her gross inattention," he said.

"They missed their normal turn off, such that she was attempting to get back to her normal route to get back to the church and it's in that context that she came to be on this road – disoriented and somewhat lost," he said.
He said his client, who had since moved to Murray Bridge, had penned a letter of apology but it was not read aloud.
Mr Ey described the intersection as "notoriously dangerous" and noted a 53-year-old man had died in an unrelated crash at the same intersection earlier this month.
Prosecutor Marie Rocca said the force of impact involved in the crash was evident from the "crumpled bonnet of the ute" and the "collapsed passenger side doors" of Habonimana’s van.
She said a term of imprisonment was the only appropriate penalty for the offending, but was not opposed to it being suspended.
At the conclusion of the hearing, Judge Joana Fuller spoke directly to Habonimana, and said she would not be sending her to prison when she returns to court to be sentenced next month.
"I can tell you now that I will not be imposing a sentence that requires you to go to jail," she said.
"I don’t know what the sentence is that I will impose but I will not be separating you from your children and making you go to jail."

articles.title: Exhibition foraged from dumps around Canberra opens at NGA
articles.author: Niki Burnside

paras.en: Despite her reputation today as one of Australia's most influential artists, Rosalie Gascoigne did not start exhibiting any of her work until she was aged 57.
Gascoigne, who created much of her work in Canberra and died in 1999, "hit the art world at just the right time," according to curator Deborah Hart.
"Art was starting to take different forms — there was installation art, minimalism, conceptual art,"
Gascoigne held her first solo exhibition in 1976 and in 1978 was invited to have a survey exhibition at the National Gallery of Victoria.
But Canberra remained the bedrock of much of her work, with many of her pieces made from materials gathered from dumps and brought back to the family home to be reshaped.

"I'm really hoping that this exhibition might generate some excitement from outside of Australia, but I wonder what they'd make of the names of the local dumps of Gundaroo, Bungendore and Captain's Flat," Dr Hart said.
Hester Gascoigne said the exhibition at the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra was made up of pieces she could remember her mother creating over the decades.
"It's quite extraordinary to see it all laid out ... to be reacquainted with works which we saw being made but haven't seen for decades, and to see the progression," Ms Gascoigne said.
Ms Gascoigne said her mother "made a game" of creating art when she was growing up, as a way of engaging children in nature.
"There was always a family competition of finding the best stone when we went for picnics down the river, and the nicest line of branch and all of that,"
"But the trips foraging to dumps were, in many respects, very serious because it was her working material."
The family home was built by Ms Gascoigne's parents with the work of her mother in mind, "so there were spaces to work and place to look at things".
"The hope was we could get access to the dining room table," she said.
"I could never understand how she could create huge things like this or like that from a very crowded, confined space."
Gascoigne's husband, Ben Gascoigne, was an astronomer, and for a time the family lived at Mount Stromlo Observatory in Canberra, where the artist did not initially have a car.
"And so she's walking across the landscape, she's getting to know this place. It really is the wellspring, the foundation of her art,"
Gallery director Nick Mitzevich said Gascoigne's works had been a part of the collection for decades.
"The National Gallery, with the great insight of the inaugural gallery director James Mollison, made our first acquisition of Rosalie Gascoigne in 1976," he said.
He said Gascoigne was an artist who "both defined art history and encouraged us to look at art in a different way".
Dr Hart said becoming a part of the NGA had been a moment of "sheer excitement" for Gascoigne.
"Suddenly she wasn't the square peg in the round hole that she felt when she brought pieces of driftwood and stones back to the mantelpiece of the house," she said.
Dr Hart quoted some of what Gascoigne had to say about her remarkable career at the exhibition's launch on Thursday:
"I think it's a basic human fear to be boxed in, and when you're an artist, you've got an expanding universe. Anything can happen."
Gascoigne continued working late into her life, retaining a youthfulness that amazed those who knew her.
"She became younger as she got older, because she grew into her true self," Dr Hart said.
The exhibition will run at the National Gallery of Australia from October 24 to February 14.

articles.title: El Niño breaks warming records in the Pacific Ocean, foreshadowing more extreme weather to come, UN says
articles.author: Olivia Le ‌Poidevin

paras.en: El Niño breaks warming records in the Pacific Ocean, foreshadowing more extreme weather to come, UN says
Floods in some regions, droughts in others as El Niño continues to gather strength

The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Wednesday.

The new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong, with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about 3.8 C above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

"We have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around [3 C] in some record El Niños before, with very substantive impacts across the world. So we are beyond that limit," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.
Celeste Saulo, World Meteorological Organization secretary-general, is warning of record temperatures during this El Niño. (Sergei Grits/The Associated Press)

El Niño is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle — a climate pattern that influences weather around the world. It tends to cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.
It is a natural climate pattern and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Niños more intense because the baseline temperature is already higher.
El Niño-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.
In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.
- Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
- El Niño-driven heat could cause half a million extra deaths, report says. Here's where
- 'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
The WMO and the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.

"This El Niño is the behemoth, it is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood," Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.
Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he said.

articles.title: El Salvador's president says military operation launched in Haiti to retrieve missing UN force members

paras.en: El Salvador's president says military operation launched in Haiti to retrieve missing UN force members
Nayib Bukele says 4 Salvadoran members of UN Gang Suppression Force were taken hostage by gangs

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday that Haitian gangs were holding hostage four Salvadoran members of an international UN-backed security force, and that he had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed.

El Salvador's military and the UN Gang Suppression Force, mandated to help Haitian police fight powerful gangs, earlier this week announced efforts to recover the missing Salvadorans, but said intense fighting in the area had limited access.

"Today, we have launched a military operation to rescue them," Bukele said in a post on X, without providing further details about the operation or identifying the group holding the Salvadorans hostage.
The Gang Suppression Force did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they leapt from a burning armoured vehicle that was ambushed by armed gangs on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince while returning from a market to their base, security officials said.

Haitian gangs have cemented their influence over the capital and expanded to surrounding regions over recent years off the back of a longstanding political vacuum, widespread extortion and a flow of illegal arms largely from the U.S.

Several nations including Chad and Sri Lanka have deployed soldiers as part of the Gang Suppression Force, which a year into its mandate has reached just over a third of its planned size and has had limited impact on Haiti's security.
Bukele said the missing men were aviation technicians, not combatants.
"Our mission consists only of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary job is to carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war," he said.
Haiti's government issued a news release Wednesday evening saying the "abduction" of the aviation technicians was an "absolute priority."

It noted that a meeting was held at the prime minister's office "to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force."
"The release of the abducted soldiers is an absolute priority, and all necessary resources are being mobilized to achieve this goal," the government said.

articles.title: U.S. Embassy says Carney government brushing off 'potential interference' in midterms
articles.author: Darren Major

paras.en: U.S. Embassy says Carney government brushing off 'potential interference' in midterms
Trump administration shares list of Canadians allegedly planning to influence elections

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa says the federal government is brushing off concerns about "potential interference in U.S. elections" after Prime Minister Mark Carney insisted that Canada is not getting involved in the American midterms.
U.S. officials have in recent weeks warned against what they describe as potential Canadian interference ahead of their Nov. 3 midterm elections.

In a release on Wednesday, the embassy suggested that the "Canadian government brushes off" the Trump administration's concerns. The release lists a number of statements by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and other officials as examples of attempts to influence the midterms.
Both Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.
"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."
Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."
"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said last week that American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the midterms.
Hoekstra pointed to Joly's comments about the strategy behind Canadian counter-tariffs and the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Reagan ad that ran in the U.S. last year.

Wednesday's embassy release listed a number of grievances that Hoekstra raised last week but also added more, including Canada's consul general in Boston, Bernadette Jordan, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates — as well Liberal MP Anthony Housefather canvassing for a Florida Democrat during a primary vote earlier this year.
About half of the instances listed on the embassy's release occurred in 2026, and a handful point to events from last year, including a federal government billboard campaign from early 2025.

The release also alleges "Canada has the second-highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country," while listing 11 Canadians who have been charged for illegally voting in past U.S. elections.
According to the release, while the alleged offences took place between 2012 and 2024 — the 11 Canadians were all charged or sentenced this year.

Joly pushed back against Hoekstra's previous comments, telling reporters last week that Canada would never engage in election interference and would "never accept that also being done to us in Canada."
Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.
Carney also told Global News last week that Canada doesn't "get ourselves involved in [foreign] elections."
Peter Navarro, one of Trump's top trade advisers, also suggested Canada could interfere in the midterms during an economic conference in Washington last month.
"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach to trade talks.
"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."
The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates running for the Senate in the two border states Navarro mentioned.
The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.
"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.
Since returning to the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump has made a number of public statements backing candidates in various countries, including Argentina and Hungary.

articles.title: Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack as suspect appears in court

paras.en: Helen Haines, an Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday, has lost both of her legs, her husband said on Wednesday.
Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

A 43-year-old suspect, Brendan N. from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Haines loses both legs after apparent attack

The independent MP underwent surgery on Monday night after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that her left leg had been amputated.
Doctors then proceeded to amputate her right leg on Wednesday after having tried to save it.
"The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines told reporters in Melbourne.
"We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape," he said.
What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?
Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. Later reports from witnesses said that after first pinning Haines against her own car, the driver reversed and rammed into her a second time.
The driver was arrested shortly after, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

The suspect's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told Magistrate Allison Vaughan on Wednesday that his client suffers from a rare neurological condition, as well as an undiagnosed mental health condition. He also said the defendant was suffering from a concussion.
Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.
Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.
"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't pull it out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.
Jefferies said he then held the man down until police arrived.
"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.
Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."
"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.
Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese
Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.
"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."
At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.
Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.
Edited by: Karl Sexton and Louis Oelofse

articles.title: Raids at far-right group's offices at European Parliament

paras.en: The third-largest alliance of parties in the European Parliament, the right-wing nationalist Patriots for Europe (PfE) group, on Wednesday said searches had been carried out at "administrative offices" at the European Parliament buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.
PfE said the searches appeared to be tied to the long-running probe into alleged misuse of funds by members of the now-disbanded Identity and Democracy (ID) Group.
PfE formed out of the ashes of ID, losing and gaining some members along the way, after the last European Parliament elections in 2024.
What did the investigative body say about the searches?

The European Public Prosecutor's Office — the independent body that investigates and prosecutes crimes against the EU budget, such as corruption or misuse of EU funds — said it searched premises in France and Belgium.
It said this was part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European Union funds by a former European Parliament group.
EPPO did not say which group was involved and said it would not publish further details for now for fear of compromising the investigation.
What did the PfE say about the searches?

PfE, meanwhile, confirmed the activity around its offices but also tried to stress its distance from the case since its rebrand and reformation — even though its constituent political parties are largely the same with the notable exception of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) now being excluded.

"Since this morning, the European Public Prosecutor's Office has been carrying out searches in administrative offices at the European Parliament in Brussels and Strasbourg. It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy Group (ID) dissolved in 2024," it wrote in a statement.
"The Patriots for Europe Group emphasizes that there is no legal continuity with the ID Group and that it is not involved in the ongoing investigations," it said.

A French member of the European Parliament for the Rassemblement National or National Rally (RN) party, Jean-Paul Garraud, said that "the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy group" were targeted.
What were the details of the ID misuse of funds probe?
European Parliament auditors concluded last year that ID members had misused at least €4.3 million (roughly $4.8 million) in EU funds during the previous legislative term from 2019 to 2024.
According to their report, the money flowed to companies close to the group and to associations supporting anti-abortion campaigners.
The case was reminiscent of, but separate from, the conviction against RN leader Marine Le Pen, herself a former MEP, that for a time looked set to stifle her bid for the French presidency.
The ID group existed for one term in the European Parliament, from 2019 to 2024. It included France's RN, Germany's AfD, Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) and Italy's Lega, among other members.

It fell apart after major internal friction during the 2024 European election campaign, not least because of dissatisfaction within the group with their lead candidate Maximilian Krah of the AfD over a number of issues — from controversial remarks about Nazi Germany through to allegations of his close allies being Russian and Chinese influence, with one of Krah's aides since convicted of spying for China.
RN, FPÖ and Lega are part of the new PfE group, which claims "no legal continuity" to the dissolved ID alliance, but the AfD was not invited to join the PfE.

PfE has 85 seats in the 719-seat European Parliament, making it the third-largest group in the chamber, but a rather distant third behind the center-right European People's Party (184) and the center-left Socialists and Democrats (135).
The European Parliament relies heavily on such groupings, which try to unite political parties from various member states with broadly comparable policy positions and political alignment.
The AfD set up a much smaller splinter far-right grouping called Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), with just 27 seats, 15 of them held by the AfD.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi at one table, without Ukraine. What Moscow wants from the proposal and why Beijing might agree.

paras.en: The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions.

Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on October 21.

Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war."

According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting.
Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine

Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia.

Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account.

According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference, referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe.

The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table.
What does China stand to gain from the talks?

Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power.

The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible.

Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play?

Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said.

Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship."

Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation.

However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia.

Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW.

He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington.
Is Putin's political survival crucial for China?
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war.

Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said.
According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way.

He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness?
Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China.
Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence.
In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak.
Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations.

He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe.
Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries.
He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said.
He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence.

"The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine.
He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground.
"China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said.

"Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war

paras.en: Mekelle, Ethiopia- In Mekelle, shops are reopening, and banks are resuming services, but residents remain anxious about what comes next. Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters retook the Tigray regional capital on October 4, as renewed fighting raised fears that the region’s fragile recovery could be derailed once again.

Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, is still recovering from the 2020–2022 war between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the region’s dominant political movement. For residents, the return of fighting has brought new uncertainty over jobs, education, security and the future.
Daily life resumes, but hardship remains.

Businesses and financial services are gradually reopening in Mekelle, but many households are struggling to afford necessities. Delayed salaries have left public employees struggling to cover food, rent and school costs, while years of conflict have depleted family savings.

“Things may be reopening, but that does not mean our problems are over. We still have expenses every day, and without our salaries, it is difficult to know how we will manage,” said Gebregziabher, a public servant in Mekelle.

The funding crisis has affected the wider public sector. In March, Tigray’s interim administration said it could no longer cover monthly salaries for about 137,000 civil servants because expected federal budget transfers had not arrived. In April, the regional finance bureau reported an 8.5-billion-birr (about $52,000) funding shortfall affecting salary payments and development projects.
For many residents, the reopening of businesses offers only a partial return to normality. Without reliable incomes and greater security, everyday expenses remain difficult to manage.

For students in Tigray, renewed fighting has revived fears of another interruption to their education. Many already lost valuable study time during the previous war and worry about falling further behind.
In Adigrat, Shewit, a grade 10 student, said uncertainty about classes and security had left him worried about his future.
“I have already lost so much time because of the war. I am afraid that if our education is disrupted again, I will lose another year and fall further behind,” he said.

Some university students have left Tigray for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, to seek transfers to other public universities. The Ministry of Education announced temporary placements at universities elsewhere in the country for students enrolled at institutions in Tigray. More than 5,000 returning students had applied by September 17–18, according to reporting on the ministry’s programme.
Abel, a third-year student at Axum University, travelled to Addis Ababa to request a transfer.

“I didn’t want to leave, but I also can’t keep putting my education on hold. I came to Addis to see if I can transfer to another university and continue my studies. I just want to finish what I started,” he said.

For students who have already lost years to conflict, the uncertainty means more than interrupted classes. It threatens to delay graduation and make an already difficult path to employment even harder.
Border communities fear a wider conflict
Near the Eritrean border, military movements and conflicting accounts of troop deployments have heightened fears that the fighting could spread beyond Tigray.

On October 8, The Associated Press reported claims by a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government that Eritrean troops had entered Adigrat earlier that week and Idaga Hamus the following day. The AP said it could not independently verify those accounts. The conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED separately reported Eritrean troops crossing the border at Zalambessa.

On October 13, Reuters reported that Ethiopian government forces had advanced into Zalambessa, citing people in contact with residents and other sources. The report said it remained unclear whether Eritrean troops or Tigrayan opposition fighters were still present in the town. The differing accounts underscored the difficulty of establishing control of individual towns as the fighting shifted.

The developments have unfolded amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara. On October 8, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, accused Eritrea of sending troops as far as 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopian territory in several areas of Tigray and appealed to the United Nations Security Council to respond.

Eritrea has denied invading Ethiopian territory. Its government said Ethiopia’s accusations amounted to a declaration of war and called on the Security Council to take action against Ethiopia. The competing claims have raised fears that renewed fighting in Tigray could lead to a direct confrontation between the two neighbours.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought on the same side during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean forces supported the federal government against the TPLF. Their deteriorating relations have added a regional dimension to the renewed conflict.
In Zalambessa, residents are watching developments with concern. One resident, who declined to be named, said the uncertainty made it difficult to know what to expect in the coming weeks.

On October 16, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, tasked with restoring public services, helping displaced people return and preparing the region for elections. The announcement followed the federal forces’ takeover of Mekelle and other major towns.

The federal government says the temporary administration will help restore stability and pave the way for elected regional leadership. The TPLF has opposed the federal advance, and it remains uncertain how effectively the new administration will operate across the region.
For residents, the immediate concerns are whether salaries will be paid, schools and health facilities will function, and displaced families will be able to return safely.
In Zalambessa, Gebrehiwot said residents knew from experience what another conflict could bring.
“People are worried because we know what war means for this area. We have already suffered enough, and nobody wants to see things reach that point again,” he said.

articles.title: Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend wall

paras.en: The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico.

The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out.
The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park.
Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, and, according to opponents of the project who have sued the administration, accounts for about 1 percent of migrant arrests.

The lawsuit, filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border.
US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order.
In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.
The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction.
The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal.

“Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.

articles.title: Brazil’s Bolsonaro challenges Lula to expand release of personal records

paras.en: Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has set out steep conditions for disclosing his personal records in response to a challenge from President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, his opponent in Sunday’s election run-off.

Bolsonaro’s campaign has said it will release the data Lula requested if the president expands his own pledge to disclose his personal records to include those of his advisers, security staff and records from companies held by Lula’s children.
Lula said on Tuesday that he would share his bank, tax and telephone records, along with those of his family, if Bolsonaro would agree to do the same.
His campaign submitted conditional authorisation to Brazil’s electoral court to release the president’s personal data.

Camilo Santana, a senator and representative of Lula’s campaign, told journalists that Lula has agreed to Bolsonaro’s new demands, and the president’s would file an official response with the court on Thursday morning.

The call from Lula on Tuesday came as both campaigns try to navigate the fallout of an explosive corruption scandal involving disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, which has implicated influential individuals and institutions across Brazil.

Bolsonaro, who narrowly leads Lula in the polls, is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering related to an investment he allegedly sought from Vorcaro. He is also under investigation in a separate probe over alleged money laundering.
The presidential hopeful denies any wrongdoing.

Brazil’s president is also linked to a corruption scandal, via his son Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, a businessman, who is accused being investigated over allegations that he unlawfully helped another businessman to gain access to the government.
Lula’s eldest son is also being investigated over his links to a businessman detained under a pension fraud probe.
Lula’s son denies the allegations, and the president has said his son would be treated like any other citizen.

articles.title: Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
articles.author: Robbie Griffiths

paras.en: Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace.

That was until Coe started researching the warming temperatures in the region. Coe had a job making videos for environmental activists, and ten years ago, when he spoke to his colleagues about the effects of climate change – and read the scientific papers himself – he started to get concerned.

"I realized that it was likely to get very, very hot in the British Midlands, even during my lifetime," Coe, 69, told NPR. "I said… I think we need to move to Scotland." A decade later, now Coe and his partner Lizzie Stoodley live on the Isle of Skye off Scotland's west coast.

There they have built a "Passivhaus" — a highly energy-efficient home — the second they have built. And they are glad they built their new home where they did. "Our decision to move seems to have been confirmed as being the right one, particularly this year," Coe told NPR.

Friends who still live further south have told the couple that the weather was "unbelievably hot" and "incredibly uncomfortable" this summer, as the United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record, with five successive heat waves and widespread drought.

But while southern regions warmed up, the weather on the Isle of Skye remained temperate. "I think there are quite a few more very hot summers I might escape by living here rather than remaining where we did," Coe said.
Susan Chinnery and her partner Steve Lewis, used to live near Milton Keynes, 50 miles north of London. But they began finding the summer months increasingly uncomfortable.

"I hate the hot weather," Chinnery told NPR. "I remember 2022 when Steve and I… we were actually sleeping outside on the patio because it was just too hot to sleep indoors." Like many British homes, their Victorian-era house was designed to keep in the warmth, and doesn't have air conditioning.

Lewis said that 2022 reminded him of the famously hot British summer of 1976, and he realised it was only going to get warmer. "I thought to myself, it's arrived," he told NPR. "This is the slow and inexorable decline into some new state."
Last year, Chinnery and Lewis moved to Westray, one of the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland, largely because of rising temperatures.

Melissa Terras also moved to Scotland, partly because of climate change. "When I mentioned climate change to people as one of the reasons why we were going to move north, people laughed," Terras told NPR. "They were like, 'What are you talking about?'"

In 2017, Terras moved her family from Letchworth Garden City, a town 40 miles north of London, to Edinburgh. A professor at the University of Edinburgh, Terras chose a house "up a hill," mindful of rising sea levels. She says more people are now thinking as she did several years ago.

The trend is also emerging in the housing market. Real estate agents in the Scottish Highlands told NPR that more buyers are citing cooler summers as a factor in their home-buying decisions. Recent figures show that house prices in Scotland rose year over year, while they fell in southeastern England and Greater London.
All over Europe, there are signs that climate is beginning to influence where many people are choosing to live, alongside factors including jobs, housing and the economy.

Scientists say Europe is the world's fastest warming continent. Large areas of Europe saw scorching temperatures this summer, with widespread wildfires, and at least 35,000 excess deaths thought to have been linked to the heat.

As climate change intensifies, countries around the world are grappling with more extreme impacts. At this year's U.N. General Assembly, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, called recent flash floods in his country "a warning to the world," urging a "culture of preparedness" for future climate crises.
Gaia Vince, a London-based journalist and author of Nomad Century, predicts climate change will drive hundreds of millions of people from hotter regions to more temperate areas this century.

The U.K. has felt the effects, too. "We've had five almost consecutive heat waves this year alone, and our infrastructure is built for a completely different climate — everything is built for a climate which no longer exists," Vince told NPR.

Britain will also see migration, Vince said, as people adapt their lifestyles and infrastructure. Wealthier individuals are already moving toward places such as Ireland and Scotland in search of a more livable climate, she said.
Vince expects a similar trend in the United States, with the Great Lakes region and Alaska potentially attracting people from farther south.
Some Americans are already making the move to Scotland. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved with his wife, Christine, last year to Golspie in the Scottish Highlands.
After experiencing wildfires in Los Angeles and hot summers while working in London, Sorensen said "something broke" inside him, and he decided he wanted to live somewhere cooler.

"Between now and 2100, there really are only a few places that you could categorize as 'best of the worst' oases if things really go to hell," Sorensen told NPR. "Certain parts of Norway, the South Island of New Zealand, maybe southern Chile down near the Lake District, maybe certain parts of Alaska — and northern Scotland."
Not so long ago, people who said they wanted to live in Scotland for the weather would have been laughed at.
But for many living farther south, it seems the joke isn't quite so funny anymore.

articles.title: Putin releases American Stephen Hubbard from Russian prison
articles.author: Charles Maynes

paras.en: Putin releases American Stephen Hubbard from Russian prison
Russian President Vladimir Putin has freed another American, 74-year-old Michigan native Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has freed another American from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump. Stephen Hubbard, who's a 74-year-old native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence in Russia after being convicted of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. His release came as White House Envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in Russia to discuss the latest U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine. NPR's Charles Maynes is on the line from Moscow. Hi there.
SUMMERS: Charles, if you could, just tell us more about Hubbard and how he ended up in a Russian prison.

MAYNES: Yeah. You know, Hubbard is a former school teacher who was detained by Russian forces in Eastern Ukraine in 2022. He'd moved there after marrying a Ukrainian woman. And after his capture, he was later sentenced in a closed trial to nearly seven years in prison, as you know, for fighting on behalf of Ukraine while in his 70s. The U.S. formally designated him wrongfully detained under the Biden administration. And amid concerns over his health and safety, the Trump White House made gaining his release a priority.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SUMMERS: Was this release a surprise, though?

MAYNES: Not really. President Trump had signaled negotiations for Hubbard's freedom were in the works in comments to journalists this week. But the reveal came during a visit today by White House Envoy Steve Witkoff to Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital, where he met with President Vladimir Putin. The reason was to discuss new proposals from the U.S. aimed at trying to find an end to the war in Ukraine. And yet, with cameras rolling during introductory remarks, Hubbard's case took center stage. Witkoff thanked Putin for arranging Hubbard's release. Putin confirmed the American was already at the airport, and then Witkoff added this.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: STEVE WITKOFF: You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir. And I salute that. I commend you, and I thank you again.
SUMMERS: I got to say, Charles, hearing Steve Witkoff describe Putin as a humanitarian - that is pretty striking.
MAYNES: Yeah. It's not the first time Witkoff has been publicly flattering Putin, but you can imagine how well that went over in Ukraine, given 4 1/2 years of war.
SUMMERS: And sticking with Hubbard for a minute here, do we know anything about his condition, how he's doing?

MAYNES: Well, state media issued footage of a smiling Hubbard shaking hands with Witkoff as the Kremlin's White House envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, looked on. Hubbard will, of course, need the full medical examination, but he seemed to look reasonably well. And Hubbard's family is happy. His son, who's an Orthodox priest named Father Joseph Coleman, thanked President Trump, as well as President Putin, for securing his father's release. And Hubbard's already on his way home.
SUMMERS: And, Charles, did the United States give up anything for Hubbard's return?

MAYNES: Well, President Trump, in a social media post celebrating the news of Hubbard's release, insisted, no. He said the U.S. hadn't given, quote, "anything in return." But, of course, Hubbard's release took place against this really extraordinary last two weeks during which Trump has made a series of gestures towards Russia and against Ukraine. He's agreed to buy previously sanctioned Russian diesel fuel. He's placed a waiver on a congressional sanctions package that he himself had signed into law. He's pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil facilities and even called for Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy's ouster.

MAYNES: Well, Trump argues this engagement with Russia, you know, these deals are part of a wider plan to keep Moscow involved in the peace negotiations and that they're in the interest of American consumers as well. You know, and there's something to show for that. Putin announced that the first shipments of Russian diesel - 60,000 tons - would be heading to the U.S. in the next few days. And a Kremlin aide said Putin had agreed to resuscitate trilateral peace talks with the U.S. and Ukraine, something he'd been refusing to do. The question is whether that's just optics or there's something really new to discuss here.
